ON YOUR TURN: 1. Roll the dice. 2. Remove enemy stones in the quantity indicated by the lower die value. 3. Place your stones on any unoccupied cells, except where prohibited as described below, in the quantity indicated by the higher die value. 4. If you completely surround an enemy singleton - enemy group of size 1 - that is, every one of its adjacent cells is occupied by one of your stones - you must immediately remove it. 5. For each enemy stone you surround and capture, you must add an additional stone of your color. It could then capture more enemy stones and require you to add yet more of your stones during your turn. 6. Prohibited placement: You may not place a stone on a cell completely surrounded by enemy stones - that is, a cell whose every adjacent cell is occupied by an enemy stone. If at any time during your turn, the only unoccupied cells are such self-capturing placements, your turn is concluded. BALANCING RULE: Black, on their first turn, places the number of stones indicated by the LOWER die value. OBJECT OF THE GAME: The game ends when the board is completely filled. Who has the most stones on the board wins. Number of players: 2 Game duration: 11 mn Complexity: 3 / 5 Play Herd and 1414 other games online. [Rating: 2/10] 2 player abstract with far too much luck involved. Especially early on, wildly different die rolls can lead to one player feeling completely out of the game. Even if they actually aren't, that isn't a state a game should put player in, especially in this genre. The main reason for this low score comes from the end of the game, though, where you can easily see that one player has the game locked down, but the dice might extend the gameplay longer than necessary. In a game with such high luck, though, simply conceding in this situation isn't necessarily correct either.

[Rating: 4/10] The luck of the die rolls can easily create a situation where it's simply impossible for a player to come back from a losing position, not due to skill, but due to luck. The fact that this game doesn't end until all the spaces are filled also doesn't help, as the stone removal mechanic can create an endgame where the outcome is inevitable, but the number of turns to finish the game is not.   Even though I was winning by a landslide, I just wanted the game to be over, and it was unclear how soon that was actually going to happen.
